title: My AI Coding Workflow That Actually Works
summary: Practitioner workflow: agents/spec/roadmap files, tests first, small PRs, independent AI review and manual merge gates.

assertions.quote: you're going to have an agents, a spec, a road map

verdicts.note: Persistent instruction files measurably steer agent behavior; overlong or contradictory ones reduce adherence.

assertions.quote: A lot of people skip this entire thing ... and that's why they get poor results

verdicts.note: Clear requirements, examples and references reliably improve agent output; the caveat is that bloated context can hurt, so curation matters.

assertions.quote: instruct it specifically to make uh a testing suite for you and then check that testing suite

verdicts.note: Agent benchmarks and practice consistently show verifiable feedback (tests, compilers) is the main driver of agent success.

assertions.quote: the big one here is acceptance criteria ... You got to let it know when it succeeds

verdicts.note: Checkable acceptance criteria give agents a stopping condition and give reviewers a test; out-of-scope lists reduce scope creep. Standard practice that carries over well to agents.

assertions.quote: LLMs always pick old versions that have tons of security problems in them

verdicts.note: Training cutoffs reliably cause stale version and model suggestions; checking against current docs is necessary.

assertions.quote: it needs to be outside of this agent

verdicts.note: Fresh-context reviewers avoid self-confirmation and context bloat; plausible and commonly practiced but little hard evidence.

assertions.quote: you forgot about what happens if there's no audio

verdicts.note: AI reviewers do catch real defects missed by humans, though with notable false-positive rates; complement, not replacement.

assertions.quote: I don't trust AI enough to just manually rubber stamp this stuff. So important to have that manual gate

verdicts.note: Given documented defect and security rates in AI code, human review before merge is standard practice (e.g. Amazon's two-person rule for AI-assisted changes); it's a sound norm.
The paper recommends careful review of AI code whatever the tool, along with static analysis, tests, security checks, and monitoring after merge.

assertions.quote: if you want to just be like, hey, I want just one prompt and have it loop a whole bunch ... that's not really a good idea

verdicts.note: Goal/loop features keep agents going through backlogs, but unattended runs drift or game checks without good verification; works when acceptance tests are strong.

assertions.quote: You're not going to be able to do it without the $100, $200 subscriptions

verdicts.note: Agentic usage is metered or rate-limited across vendors; heavy users routinely hit limits or pay usage overages.

assertions.quote: I know I'm using way more compute than the cost that I pay them

verdicts.note: Heavy users clearly consume more compute than flat fees cover, which is why vendors added weekly limits; whether plans are below cost on average is not public.

assertions.quote: think about chunking those into smaller poll requests

verdicts.note: Small batches with fast feedback are a strong DORA predictor of delivery performance; DORA 2024 linked AI to larger batches and lower stability.

assertions.quote: even if you take the LLM out of this, this is just a good workflow for developing software

verdicts.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing engineering practices; strong fundamentals predict AI benefit.
